summary: At just 1.2 square miles, Cherryland packs nearly 15,000 people into a density north of 12,000 per square mile — denser than many incorporated Bay Area cities, yet it isn't actually a city at all but an unincorporated census-designated place in Alameda County, wedged between Hayward and San Lorenzo on the flat East Bay plain. That peculiar status means county services rather than a city council, which shapes everything from road maintenance to park planning. The terrain is uniformly flat here, with the western hills of Hayward rising visibly to the east and San Francisco Bay a short drive west, but Cherryland itself sits squarely on the valley floor without elevation drama. With a median home value around $654,200 against a median household income of roughly $84,800, the price-to-income ratio lands near 7.7 — stretching ownership out of comfortable reach at the median without significant down-payment wealth, while rents averaging $2,109 consume about 30% of that same median income, right at the conventional affordability threshold. The area functions primarily as a commuter base; BART's Hayward station sits just outside the boundary, funneling workers toward Oakland, San Francisco, and the Silicon Valley corridor. Year-round highs averaging 67°F with nine hours of daily sunshine deliver mild, fog-buffered seasons without the inland heat spikes of the Tri-Valley. Cherryland's defining tension is geographic: dense enough to feel urban, small enough to lack its own civic infrastructure, and positioned in one of the most expensive metro areas in the country without the income base to match.
